extracted.intended_audience: copyright policymakers, practitioners, and creators using AI-generated content
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when AI-generated or AI-assisted materials qualify for copyright protection, focusing on human authorship, expressive inputs, selection/arrangement, and international approaches. Applies to registration and legal analysis of works containing AI-generated elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompts alone do not provide sufficient human control for authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompts essentially function as instructions that convey unprotectible ideas; while highly detailed prompts could contain the user’s desired expressive elements, at present they do not control how the AI system processes them in generating the output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases regarding joint authorship support this conclusion: providing detailed directions without influence over how those directions are executed is insufficient. The Office’s example (prompt for a cat image) shows prompts may specify subject, style, and placement yet leave many expressive elements unspecified; identical prompts can produce different outputs, indicating lack of human control. Citations: Payday; CCNV; third circuit and other authorities. If future technology allows prompts to constrain expressive elements more fully, the analysis may change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of human control (control over expressive elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship depends on the degree to which a human can constrain or channel the program’s processing so that human contribution determines expressive elements of the output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue is not mere unpredictability but whether the human is 'principally responsible for the execution' and the determination of expressive elements (analogies: Jackson Pollock, nature photographer). Foreseeability and predictability of results may bear on control in cases where a limited range of specific expressive output is objectively foreseeable. See Kernochan Center, DMLA, MPA, INTA comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship by adoption is insufficient to establish authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory that a user can adopt unplanned or unexpected variations in output (i.e., 'authorship by adoption') does not itself confer copyright authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters and the Office note that merely adopting or selecting an outcome produced by the system is more akin to curating or 'selection among offered options' than to original authorship. Authorities (e.g., Ginsburg & Budiardjo discussion and case law) caution that recognizing adoption as authorship would vest adopters with rights in ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetitive prompting, effort, or 'sweat of the brow' do not create authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The time, expense, or demonstrable human effort involved in iteratively revising prompts is irrelevant to copyright, which protects original authorship rather than hard work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly revising and submitting prompts is characterized as 're-rolling the dice' and does not appear materially different from inputting a single prompt; selection of a final output after many attempts reflects acceptance of the system’s interpretation rather than authorship. Citation: Feist v. Rural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive inputs (human-created inputs retained in output confer protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a human author inputs their own copyrightable work (text, image, audio, video) and that work is perceptible in the AI output, the human-authored portion of the output is protectable as their authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rose Enigma—hand-drawn illustration used as input whose expressive elements (mask outline, rose arrangement, relative facial feature placement) were perceptible in the output; Office registered the applicant’s unaltered human pictorial authorship and excluded non-human expression. Protection extends to perceptible human expression and may cover selection/coordination of human-authored and AI-generated material (analogous to derivative work protection for additions by a later author). Citations: DMLA, Pearson, NMPA comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection, coordination, arrangement, and modification can create human authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: A human may claim copyright for the resulting work where they select, coordinate, arrange, or modify AI-generated material in a sufficiently creative way to meet the originality standard (Feist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office found compilation protection where images and human-authored text were selected and arranged creatively (Zarya of the Dawn example). Modifying AI-generated output (editing, adapting, enhancing) may contribute new authorship assessed like editorial changes to pre-existing works. Tools (e.g., Midjourney’s Vary Region/Remix, OpenAI Canvas) can enable users to exert such control. However, whether modifications meet Feist is case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum creativity threshold / de minimis selection rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection, coordination, or arrangement must clear a minimal creativity threshold; the selection of only two or three elements is generally insufficient for copyright protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to COMPENDIUM (THIRD) § 312.2 and legislative history noting compilations with relatively few elements typically do not qualify (selection is necessarily de minimis). This limits registration claims where only a very small number of AI elements are chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI cannot be an author, form intent, or enter binding contracts (no joint works or works made for hire)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI systems are not authors under copyright law: they cannot form intent to merge their output with a user’s contributions, nor can they enter into binding contracts; therefore AI cannot be a joint author or a party for works made for hire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consequence means entirely AI-generated outputs lack human authorship; any human claim must rest on human contributions. Citations: Kernochan Center comments; Thaler litigation briefs; statutory framework for work made for hire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of protection for human contributions in AI-generated outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protection for works containing human inputs and AI-generated elements extends only to the human-contributed material (perceptible human expression) and to the human author’s selection, coordination, and arrangement — not to AI-generated elements standing alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to derivative works: protection covers material added by the later human author and does not affect the public domain status of pre-existing material. Office registrations have annotated claims to limit protection to unaltered human-authored elements when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of AI-generated elements in larger human-authored works does not preclude protection of the larger work
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of AI-generated special effects or background artwork within a larger human-authored work does not prevent the larger work from being copyrightable, even if the AI elements themselves are not separately protectable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a film including AI-generated effects remains copyrightable as a whole so long as the human-authored elements meet originality requirements; analogous guidance in AI Registration Guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint authorship / hiring-artist analogy (control over execution vs mechanical transcription)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case law distinguishes between providing directions that produce 'rote or mechanical transcription' (which may allow the delegating party to claim authorship) and situations where the executing party exercises intellectual modification or enhancement (which precludes such a claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a person hires a human artist, the hiring party can oversee and understand the artist’s contribution; that oversight may affect authorship. By contrast, when instructing an AI, the user generally cannot oversee or understand how the system implements the instructions — weighing against user authorship. Citations: Andrien, Payday, CCNV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreseeability / predictability of AI results may inform authorship in limited-range cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a user’s input and starting materials make a limited range of specific expressive outputs objectively foreseeable, foreseeability of the AI’s results may bear on whether the user’s contribution supports authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments (DMLA, Kernochan, MPA) suggest foreseeability and control are relevant in cases with objectively foreseeable outputs; however, foreseeability alone does not automatically create authorship and must be evaluated with other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: International approaches: many jurisdictions require human authorship or significant human input
rubrics_metrics.description: Other countries’ guidance largely holds that copyright requires human authorship or substantial human contribution; approaches and tests vary by jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Korea: only a natural person can be an author; copyright registration impossible if a human did not contribute creatively to expressive form (Korean Guide). Japan: case-by-case determination using factors — (1) amount/content of instructions and input prompts; (2) number of generation attempts; (3) selection by user from multiple outputs; (4) subsequent human additions/corrections. China: Beijing Internet Court found an image created using Stable Diffusion protectable based on extensive prompts and subsequent adjustments (over 150 prompts demonstrated 'intellectual achievements'). EU member states: majority view that current copyright principles suffice and AI-generated content may be eligible only if human input was significant. UK: statutory regime designates a 'person by whom the arrangements are made' as author for computer-generated works (CDPA §§178, 9(3)).
